h: The wind turns at Ramlila Maidan: anger is now becoming organisation
dek: For Zoya Hasan, the real news of the 1 November rally is not the crowd but a mood that is demanding answers from both the government and the Election Commission.
body: JNU professor emerita Zoya Hasan begins with the wave rising against the right across the world, from the US midterm elections to Lula's win in Brazil and the government brought down by students in Serbia. The picture in India is more tangled, because the BJP's organisation runs very deep, yet in her view politics is no longer one-sided.

According to the writer, the mood at the 1 November 'Chalo Dilli' rally mattered more than the head count. The marches of 12 October and 1 November show that the Congress organisation is moving again and that Rahul Gandhi has become the main voice of this unease. She sees the way the INDIA alliance parties kept step with the Congress as unusual unity.

The root of the grievance is the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls. According to the piece, more than 13 crore names were left out of the draft rolls, while the 'infiltration' used to justify all this turned up only about 1,600 cases among 9.86 crore voters in six states. The burden of proof has shifted from the state to the ordinary voter. Complaints about unemployment, rising prices, the farm crisis and women's safety have also joined this issue.

Hasan says this crowd rose above the Hindu-Muslim divide, and that the Cockroach Janata Party, left student groups and citizens' groups made it bigger than the parties. But she also lists the weaknesses: the Cockroach Janata Party gave its support but did not come on stage, and a shared agenda is yet to be built.

Her sharpest argument is about Parliament. The government says Parliament is the place for debate, but there a discussion on 'vote theft' is put off and notices to remove the Chief Election Commissioner are rejected, while protest on the street is blocked. The writer says this rally could also slow down SIR, delimitation and 'One Nation One Election'.
nazar: This piece is not a celebration written in excitement but a cool reckoning: the figure of 1,600 against 13 crore shows by itself how hollow the 'infiltration' argument was. Hasan's most important point is that when the doors of Parliament are shut and the streets are barricaded, the government is really wiping out the very space for dissent.
But her warning matters just as much. A crowd can change the mood, not the roll. The movement now also has to do the concrete work of getting every deleted name added back.
sawal: If debate in Parliament is shut down, what road is left except the street?
ref: Special Intensive Revision (SIR)

The Election Commission's drive to check voter rolls afresh.
The opposition alleges that crores of valid names were cut in it.
The India Cable

A newsletter from The Wire and Galileo Ideas.
This piece first appeared there.
ank: names left out of the draft rolls
photo_note: Representative image: a student protest march

h: The government has trapped itself with Gyanesh Kumar
dek: Jagdish Rattanani says that after the 1 November rally, neither the government nor the opposition has a way to step back.
lang: Hindi (a piece carried from The Billion Press syndicate; original language not stated)
body: Senior journalist Jagdish Rattanani argues that the easiest path for the government was to distance itself from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, even if only for show. That did not happen, and now defending the wholesale deletion of names during SIR has become almost impossible.

According to the writer, the joint rally of 1 November changed the map of the game. Elections in five states, including Uttar Pradesh, are due in early 2027, and talk of a boycott is rising. Now either the government bears the embarrassment of removing Kumar, or the opposition stays out of elections held under his watch, which would turn the elections into a farce. He sees no middle path.

He finds the BJP's response to the rally weak: complaints about the crowd and about disruption to Diwali shopping, and silence on the real question. In his view, an image built over ten years is cracking fast on the issue of 'vote theft', and the root of this lies in a style of communication that hammers home everything like propaganda.

The most interesting part of the piece is about the 2024 Pew survey, in which 85 percent of Indians said they favoured rule by a strong leader or the army. Rattanani says that people may want tough rule in theory, but everyday rights matter more. For decades workers went door to door adding names, SIR cut names just as easily, and that is what created fear.

In the end he warns that taking down social media posts, heavy policing and withdrawing recognition of Jantar Mantar in the middle of the movement are signs of a crackdown. Still, the unity of the opposition and people's resolve to protect their vote give him hope.
nazar: The strength of this piece is the Pew survey twist: the same public said to want a 'strong leader' is out on the street when its vote is taken away. This argument, which sees democracy as an everyday right rather than a textbook ideal, takes the debate beyond slogans.
The piece is certainly hasty on the boycott. A boycott is the opposition's last weapon, but the writer himself admits it is not clear who it would hurt.
sawal: Would boycotting the election give the opposition strength, or leave the field empty?
ref: SIR

The Special Intensive Revision of voter rolls.
The opposition alleges that names of valid voters were cut on a large scale.
The Billion Press

A syndicate service that distributes columns.
The same piece appears in several newspapers.

h: Saamana: echoes of 1975 at Ramlila Maidan again
dek: An editorial in the Shiv Sena (Uddhav) paper links the 1 November rally to the JP movement and demands that Modi, Shah and Gyanesh Kumar all go.
body: This Saamana editorial is written without any hedging. It says that on 1 November lakhs of people from across the country reached Ramlila Maidan at Rahul Gandhi's 'Chalo Dilli' call, while BJP leaders kept putting the crowd at five or six thousand. The paper sees this as a sign of fear and claims that Delhi has not seen such a large political gathering in fifty years.

The editorial recalls that on Sunday the roads had barricades and heavy police, yet the ground and the roads around it filled up. When Amit Shah called 'Chalo Dilli' an invitation to anarchy, the paper asks why the same unease is not visible over Chinese incursions in Arunachal, the violence in Manipur and law and order in Bengal and Maharashtra.

The biggest argument comes from history. In 1975 JP called for change from this same ground, and the editorial sees the same anger and the same insistence on 'regime change' this time too. It pushes forward Rahul Gandhi's charge that the BJP lost in 2024 and came back to power with Gyanesh Kumar's help.

The paper mocks Shah's statement on infiltrators: if all 13.5 crore names cut from the roll were Bangladeshis, that is the Home Minister's failure and the Prime Minister should remove him. Citing the objections of two election commissioners, it says Gyanesh Kumar is clinging to his chair.
The conclusion is clear: the message of the rally is that Modi, Shah and Gyanesh Kumar must go, and the editorial says this ground will once again become the base for a big change.
nazar: This editorial is less analysis and more a war drum, and that is what makes it important: a major opposition party in Maharashtra now openly calls this movement a fight to change the government. The crowd figures and claims like 'the biggest gathering in 50 years' are the paper's own, and should be read that way.

The comparison with 1975 is powerful, but also incomplete. The JP movement was followed by the Emergency. For the people on the street today, the real question is how far this echo can carry at a time when Jantar Mantar's recognition has been taken away and people are being detained.
sawal: Can the crowd at Ramlila Maidan win back the voter roll?
ref: JP movement

The 1974-75 movement led by Jayaprakash Narayan.
The Emergency was imposed after the rally at Ramlila Maidan on 25 June 1975.
Dopahar Ka Saamana

The Shiv Sena's Hindi paper, companion to the Marathi 'Saamana'.
Its editorials state the party line.
photo_note: Representative image: India Gate at night

h: Harishankar Vyas: Trump's mistake, the same result in India?
dek: The editor of Naya India compares India with the US midterm elections and says attempts at vote rigging can backfire.
body: Harishankar Vyas opens his column with a sharp question: how many crore anti-BJP voters can be pushed off the roll through SIR with the help of officers like Gyanesh Kumar? According to the writer, about 13 crore names have already been removed from the old rolls, while the noise about 3 crore Bangladeshis was not backed by even 3 lakh proven cases.

He expects Modi and Shah to ignore the objections and keep preparing for 2029 with booth management, delimitation and women's reservation. This is where he brings in the American example. Trump and his party also pushed hard on the election process, voter data and registration, and redrew boundaries in eight states, yet in the recent midterm elections their candidates lost in places like Texas, Florida and Georgia.

The writer explains that in America elections are run by state commissions. The Trump administration and its allies filed many petitions in court, and the Justice Department filed about 31 lawsuits for voter data, but most were dismissed and state officials did not bend under pressure. He compares this with how, before the Bengal election, lakhs of voters were denied their right with the help of the courts.

Vyas concludes that when the intent to rig becomes visible to people, the biggest anger rises in the strongholds themselves. He says that since the rise of the 'Cockroach Party' the same kind of irritation is building in homes and among young men and women, and he is confident that, as in America, democracy will come alive again in India.
nazar: That a veteran editor like Vyas says 'vote rigging' is the last prop left for those in power is news in itself. The comparison with America is encouraging, but the big difference between the two systems is the one he himself points out: there, state commissions and courts did not bow to the centre.
The figures in the piece are the writer's own, and their source is not given. So a figure like 13 crore should be read as a claim.
sawal: Which institution in India can keep a check on the Election Commission?
ref: Delimitation

Redrawing the boundaries of constituencies based on population.
In America this is called redistricting.

h: Gyanesh Kumar is now a burden on Modi, but hard to remove
dek: Senior journalist Manish Chhibber says the government is caught in a trap where keeping the Chief Election Commissioner is costly, and so is removing him.
lang: Urdu (published on The Wire Urdu; original language not stated)
body: Manish Chhibber begins with Modi's political sense. He says the Prime Minister is skilled at reading the mood and public perception, and that this skill has brought him win after win. So he must know that Gyanesh Kumar has now become a burden for the government and for himself.

The writer claims that trust in the Chief Election Commissioner has fallen so low that even Modi's loyal supporters do not defend him in family and friends' WhatsApp groups. Amid the Indian Express revelations and protests that grow despite police crackdowns, explanations and new narratives are not working. When even pro-government anchors start asking questions and peaceful Gen Z protesters face action, things must be seen as having gone bad.

Plain political sense says: get rid of an ally who has become a burden, and quickly. But Chhibber points out that this is not like dropping a minister. A minister like Dharmendra Pradhan can easily resign, but the Chief Election Commissioner heads an institution seen as independent. His exit under pressure would cast a shadow on every election held under his watch.

The second fear is that the protesters will not stop at Gyanesh Kumar, and their next target will be much bigger. And the third is the message it would send to the bureaucracy and the police, who, the writer says, bend the rules to please their political masters.
The writer concludes that Gyanesh Kumar's time is up, but the government is in a tight noose, and this is where Modi's political sense will face its real test.
nazar: This piece is not sloganeering but an attempt to read the arithmetic inside power, and its sharpest point comes at the end: saving Gyanesh Kumar is really a promise to the officers who bend the rules for those in power. If that is right, the fight is not over one chair but over the whole system of rewards and punishments.
The point about WhatsApp groups is the writer's own experience, not a survey. Still, it is an interesting sign that the debate has now reached supporters' homes.
sawal: If the Chief Election Commissioner goes, who will account for the past elections?
ref: Removing the Chief Election Commissioner

Under Article 324 of the Constitution, only by a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.
The process is like removing a Supreme Court judge.

h: The Commission's somersaults on Form 6: a fix is not enough, accountability is needed
dek: A Free Press Journal editorial asks who imposed a question with a disputed legal basis on voter registration, and why.
body: The Election Commission has reversed itself several times on Form 6, the application to get a name added to the voter roll. The paper says the matter is not about an online question, but about how a constitutional body changes the rules for becoming a voter.

In July a declaration linked to SIR was added to Form 6 on the Commission's ECINet portal, asking whether the applicant, their parents or grandparents had been listed in an earlier intensive revision. On paper it was not required, but the form could not be submitted without an answer. The editorial says that in May two election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had already objected in writing that a statutory form cannot be changed without an amendment. Sandhu called it illegal, yet the condition stayed.

After that the explanations kept changing. On 26 September the Commission said the declaration would stay during SIR. The Supreme Court said it had neither approved nor rejected the changed form. According to the Commission's affidavit, on 21 October it was decided to separate the declaration from the form, and the reason given was that this saved a second OTP. The paper's reply is that convenience cannot settle a question of legal rights.

The editorial also accepts that correcting mistakes is part of running things. But it demands to be told who approved the original change, why the objections were ignored, and what is in place so it does not happen again. The verdict is clear: fixing the form is not enough, trust will return only through accountability.
nazar: This editorial comes from a mainstream Mumbai paper, and that is where its importance lies: the questions being raised as slogans on the street are now reaching editorial pages in measured legal language.

The sharpest point is that two of the Commission's own members had sounded the alarm back in May. Who will answer for the people who left their applications incomplete for months because of this condition?
sawal: Why was the written objection of two commissioners kept buried for months?
ref: Form 6

The statutory application to add a new name to the voter roll.
It is laid down under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
ECINet

The Election Commission's integrated digital portal.
The disputed declaration was added to Form 6 on it.

h: The Barakhamba Road march: what a writer saw from inside the crowd
dek: Back from the 12 October march, Mukul Kesavan asks why the Congress and older parties make no room for a new, young leadership.
body: This essay by historian and writer Mukul Kesavan first appeared in Frontline. Before going to the 12 October march against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, he checks the routes, because two days earlier the police had come down hard on a Cockroach Janata Party protest. On Barakhamba Road he sees Samajwadi caps, AISA's red flags and the tricolour, and the real energy is not in the Youth Congress but in AISA's young groups, mostly made up of young women.

Estimates of the crowd ranged from two thousand to one lakh, and the writer settles on tens of thousands. He says the July protest at Jantar Mantar was denser and more spontaneous, while this march seemed arranged from the top, with leaders arriving in AC buses. He admits that what one sees with one's own eyes and social media pictures now blend into each other.

A large part of the essay is about leadership. The Cockroach Janata Party's co-convenors Dipke and Ranka came from the Aam Aadmi Party, and the writer says the Congress kept its distance from them, while Rahul Gandhi's sympathy came late and went mostly to AISA's Neha Bora. Kesavan argues that in a party whose top posts are in the hands of a family, it is hard to make room for awkward, new young leaders.

He also mentions AAP's decline, in which, by his account, it stayed silent on moments like the Delhi riots and Jahangirpuri. The Shaheen Bagh movement could not spread beyond Muslims, while this movement seems to touch everyone. His question is whether the shared frustration of having to prove citizenship can build solidarity. In the end he asks readers not to look down on these activists, because civil disobedience has opened up space for dissent.
nazar: This is a diary written with a cool head, with praise and with scratches too. Kesavan's most useful question is which house the leadership born on the street will go to, since old parties are afraid to take it in and the record of new parties does not inspire trust.

The piece is three weeks old, but after Ramlila Maidan the same question has become sharper: a stage without the Cockroach Janata Party, and the Cockroach Janata Party without a stage, are both incomplete.
sawal: Which party will young leaders who rose from the street find a home in?
ref: AISA

All India Students' Association, the student group linked to the CPI (ML) Liberation.
Neha Bora is its president.
Shaheen Bagh

The 2019-20 sit-in in Delhi against the citizenship law.
It was led mostly by Muslim women.

h: The other side's case: the Commission's affidavit and the 'Congress con'
dek: In Open magazine, Rajeev Deshpande argues that the 'vote theft' case is weak after the Commission's affidavit, but his own piece leaves many questions unanswered.
body: This piece is worth reading because it lays out the most organised argument against the movement. Rajeev Deshpande builds on the Election Commission's affidavit filed in the Supreme Court on 26 October by Deputy Election Commissioner Bhanu Prakash Yeturu. The Commission says this is the unanimous decision of all three commissioners, and that the claim that Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi objected 14 times in ten months is false.

The affidavit says the petitions rest on one newspaper report, that Form 6 was not changed but an online declaration was added to help voters, and that the talk of removing 13 crore names is 'highly misleading', because those cut include the dead, people who have moved elsewhere and duplicate entries. The writer also recalls that the Supreme Court has upheld EVMs several times since 2017.

Deshpande says there is little evidence and many accusations. On the claim that 416 names were wrongly cut at four booths in Trilokpuri, he says a booth has more than a thousand voters and the reasons for deletion are not clear. He also accuses Rahul Gandhi of drifting towards 'fringe' politics alongside people like Yogendra Yadav, Prashant Bhushan, Jean Dreze and Aruna Roy.

The writer concludes that cleaning the roll is necessary, that stopping SIR would mean protecting a vote bank, and that the attack on the Commission is really part of a larger campaign to delegitimise the Modi government. The next hearing in the case is on 17 November.
nazar: This piece is here because the movement should know the strongest argument against it. But its weaknesses are clear too: it treats the affidavit as almost the final truth, when that very affidavit is yet to be tested in court. And the piece leaves out that the Form 6 declaration, described as 'help', had to be answered before an application could be submitted.
Calling every deleted name 'dead, moved or duplicate' is not an answer either; the demand for evidence should apply equally to both sides.
sawal: Why does the Commission not make public the reason for every deleted name?
ref: Section 18, Election Commissioners Act 2023

A provision on how the Commission divides its work and takes decisions.
The Commission relied on it to call the two commissioners' objections normal procedure.
Open

An English weekly magazine published from Delhi.
Its stance is generally seen as close to the government.

h: Poverty has fallen, but by how much? Questions over World Bank figures
dek: Economist Santosh Mehrotra says the claims of a huge drop in poverty in India rest on surveys that do not match the older ones at all.
body: The World Bank claims that extreme poverty in India has fallen from 27.1 percent in 2011 to 2.6 percent. Santosh Mehrotra, a former professor at JNU, finds this picture misleading. His first objection is about method: in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 consumption surveys, households were visited three separate times, and the value of free goods and services was also added, whereas until 2011-12 there was a single visit. Changes like this record higher spending, and poverty automatically looks lower.

The writer points out that after 2014 the government never set its own poverty line, as the Planning Commission used to, and now World Bank estimates are relied on. The same doubt applies to NITI Aayog's multidimensional poverty index. The World Bank did not include any measure of health in its multidimensional estimate, and counted only access to facilities, not outcomes.

Then he compares the economy's record. Between 2004 and 2014 the average growth rate was 7.8 percent, investment reached 32 to 38 percent of GDP, and about 75 lakh non-farm jobs were created every year. In this same period the total number of poor people fell for the first time. After 2014 growth was 6.2 percent, and demonetisation, GST and the lockdown broke employment in the informal sector and small industries.

The World Bank speaks of 13.4 crore jobs between 2017 and 2023, especially for women. The writer says 6.5 crore of these people went back to farming, and many women were counted as unpaid workers on family farms. From 2017 to 2025, real wages stayed flat in both villages and cities.
His conclusion is simple: poverty may have fallen, but no one knows by how much. The country needs 1.2 crore non-farm jobs every year for the next twenty years.
nazar: The poverty figure is not just a count; it is the foundation of policy. If the poor almost vanish on paper, it becomes easy to find an excuse to cut spending on rations, MGNREGA (the rural job guarantee scheme) and social security. In a country where women are going back to the fields without wages and wages have been flat for eight years, what is needed before any celebration is a reliable poverty line of its own.
sawal: How was a woman who went back to the fields without wages counted as out of poverty?
ref: Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES)
A survey by the National Statistics Office that shows how much households spend on what. Most poverty estimates rest on it.
Tendulkar line
The poverty line suggested by the Suresh Tendulkar committee in 2009. A big fall in the number of poor people between 2004 and 2012 was measured by it.

h: Where do boys learn their lessons in power?
dek: After two attacks on girls in schools, a gender scholar looks at the lessons from home, school, cinema and mobile screens that teach boys to dominate.
body: At a school in Andhra Pradesh's Anantapur district, a 21-year-old man is alleged to have attacked a 15-year-old girl with a chainsaw, and a second girl who came to save her was also hurt. A few days earlier, at a school in Panchkula, an eight-year-old boy was accused of seriously injuring a six-year-old girl. Anjitha Gopi says plainly that the two cases are different and there is no evidence linking them to any film or influencer. The real question is: how do boys learn that being a man and being powerful are the same thing?

It starts at home: a son is allowed out late at night, his anger is called a phase, and a daughter's anger is called rudeness. Citing a study of teenagers and parents in Haryana, the writer says children's thinking is deeply tied to their parents', but conversations in class can change it.

In school and among friends, gentleness is mocked and dominance is cheered. Cinema adds fuel: the wounded, dangerous lover of 'Darr' and 'Anjaam', the stalking despite refusal in 'Raanjhanaa', and the aggression of 'Animal'. She mentions an Oxfam India study that says films weaken a woman's right to say 'no'.

Now these scenes reach phones as reels and memes. The writer gives the example of Kerala gamer YouTuber 'Thoppi', who was popular with schoolchildren despite his abusive language. The most dangerous turn comes when a woman's freedom starts to feel like a blow to a man's honour, and being rejected becomes humiliation.

She does not see taking away phones or simply blaming influencers as the answer. Families should look at how they share out freedom, schools should take consent and how friends treat each other seriously, and there should be spaces where a boy showing weakness is not seen as losing.
nazar: After every violent incident it is easy to blame the mobile phone or one film, because it spares home and school from looking in the mirror. This piece holds up that mirror. Consent and equality are still discussed with hesitation in school curricula, even though this is the most solid way to keep girls safe.
sawal: Why is a son's anger called 'a phase' and a daughter's called rudeness?
ref: Manosphere
A web of male-supremacist groups and forums spread across the internet, which paints women's equality as a threat to men. Researcher Debbie Ging has done a lot of work on it.
'Sigma male'
A term popular on social media that builds an ideal of a man who is a loner, carefree and bows to no one.

h: Aligarh gets its students' union back, with an equal share for women
dek: In the AMU students' union election, held after eight years, a woman student became vice president for the first time and women won half the cabinet seats.
body: Aligarh Muslim University held students' union elections after eight years. Noman Ashraf was elected president and Mohammad Hamdan secretary, and Nashra became vice president, the first woman student to reach the post, according to the writer. The ten-member cabinet has five women and five men, one student with a disability and two students from Kerala.

Midhat Fatima does not see this result as a sudden change. She links it to the CAA-NRC protests and Shaheen Bagh, where Muslim women's public leadership entered the national debate. She also remembers the women students who cleared the way earlier: Ghazala Ahmad, who made it to the cabinet in 2016-17, Amina Irshad, who contested for president, and Shaheen Parveen and Areeba Dilshad, who campaigned in the niqab and won.

What stands out for the writer is that Nashra also got strong support from faculties with more male voters, such as the engineering faculty and the Boys' Polytechnic. This breaks the belief that a male-majority electorate will not accept a woman leader.

She rejects two kinds of stories. One is the right-wing view that paints Muslim institutions as backward, and the other is the liberal-left claim that wants to hold the contract for Muslim women's freedom. She says these women do not need any outside 'guide'; they can stand by their own principles and contest and win elections.

The piece also mentions Afreen Fatima, president of the Women's College students' union in 2018-19, who later became a well-known voice of the anti-CAA movement. According to the writer, this victory belongs to everyone who fought before, even those who lost.
nazar: At a time when students' union elections on many campuses across the country have been put off for years and Muslim institutions are repeatedly placed under suspicion, this result from Aligarh offers a different picture. Learning democracy begins on campus, and here voters chose equality themselves, not because anyone told them to.
sawal: Why did the boys of the engineering faculty vote for a woman student?
ref: AMU Students' Union (AMUSU)
The elected student body of Aligarh Muslim University, with a history of over a hundred years. According to the piece, its elections were held after eight years.
Shaheen Bagh
The Delhi neighbourhood where Muslim women held a months-long sit-in against the Citizenship Amendment Act in 2019-20. The movement became a model for similar sit-ins across the country.

h: In Israel's election, the Palestinian vote became a shared front
dek: A Palestinian activist from Jaffa argues that Palestinians with Israeli citizenship turned their vote into a way of standing with Gaza and the West Bank.
body: Even before this piece was published, its writer, Jaffa community activist and former city councillor Abed Abou Shhadeh, was taken from his home by the Israeli police and the Shin Bet. According to the magazine, he is being investigated for 'contact with a foreign agent', and the court has extended his custody until 8 November. The piece was written before his arrest.

The writer starts with Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor's idea of 'end times fascism': power justifies dictatorship by showing the fear of doomsday. He says that a few days before the election Netanyahu shared an AI image of an atom bomb falling on Tel Aviv, as if only he could save the world.

This time Palestinians in Gaza, the West Bank and in prisons also asked Palestinian citizens of Israel to vote. The writer lists the reasons: the failure of the Palestinian national project, the sorry state of their own politics, the silence of Arab countries on Gaza, and the danger of the current government. Smotrich had promised to bring West Bank methods to this side of the Green Line, but the writer says the blurring of the border also had the opposite effect: people in the occupied territories have now become participants in Palestinian politics inside Israel.

According to the writer, Palestinian citizens voted in record numbers, mostly for the Joint List, and many who had boycotted for years also went to the polls this time. He claims the Netanyahu government's defeat would not have been possible without these votes. The citizenship that the state tried to hollow out has now become a tool of influence.

He sees the way forward in equal citizenship in one state, where the separate identity and rights of two nations are recognised. In his view the two-state solution has failed in practice, and endless war is dangerous for Israelis too.
nazar: In the week this piece was published, its writer was in custody. That alone shows how much power fears voices that turn the vote into resistance. In India too, where the minority vote is looked at with suspicion, this piece is a reminder that citizenship does not mean just papers, but a share in decisions.
sawal: Why is the writer of the vote that defeated Netanyahu in custody?
ref: Green Line

The 1949 ceasefire line that separates Israel from the West Bank and Gaza.
Palestinians living within it are citizens of Israel.
Joint List

The joint electoral front of Palestinian-Arab parties in Israel.
It has been the biggest voice of Arab citizens in the Knesset.

h: American politics after Trump: a Republican strategist's confession
dek: A veteran Republican reads his party's crushing defeat in the midterm elections as a rejection of Trumpism.
body: Republican strategist John Feehery starts with the win of Texas's new senator James Talarico, the first Democrat in about forty years to win a Senate seat from Texas. Talarico had said that people are tired of being set against one another. Feehery disagrees with his politics, but not with this.

He recalls that ten years ago Trump built a movement by giving rivals mocking nicknames, holding wrestling-style rallies and fanning anger against the elite. Angry voters came to him on the promise of stopping illegal immigration and bringing back factory jobs. After the 2020 defeat, even the claim of rigging and the Capitol Hill incident could not stop him, and he returned in 2024.

Feehery says the wind turned this time. People wanted relief from rising prices and fuel costs, while the promise to stay out of foreign wars broke with the attack on Iran. In the name of immigration, even school coaches, Uber drivers and domestic workers were caught and deported. Women, Hispanic, Asian, Arab and Black voters, and educated people in the Midwest, drifted away.

The result was that Republicans of every kind lost, hardline Trump supporters and moderates alike. The writer calls it a total wipeout for the party and says it is not an endorsement of Democratic policies but a rejection of Trumpism.

He concludes that Republicans will have to change their language and promises, because government runs on coalitions, not insults. Still, he doubts that the old, decent kind of disagreement will fully return.
nazar: This criticism comes not from a rival but from inside the house, and that is why it matters. But it is also worth noting that while counting Trump's failures, the writer says little about the responsibility of the party that stood by him for ten years. The lesson for India is clear: politics built on hate and spectacle eventually has to answer on prices and jobs.
sawal: The party that stood by Trump for ten years: who will it apologise to now?
ref: Midterm elections (midterms)

Congressional elections held in the middle of a US president's four-year term.
All seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of Senate seats are at stake.
MAGA

'Make America Great Again', Trump's slogan and the movement of his supporters.
It rests on opposition to immigration and a protectionist trade policy.

h: How politics broke friendships and homes in Bangladesh
dek: A Dhaka University teacher asks why, when parties switch alliances, it is their supporters who lose their relationships.
body: Umme Wara, who teaches criminology at Dhaka University, begins with an American survey. Researchers at the University of California, Irvine spoke to about 3,800 people in May 2026 and found that more than a third of Americans have lost a friend, relative or partner over political differences. The writer says that in Bangladesh too, this 'political breakup' has now reached homes.

She traces the roots of this divide to 1971, then through BAKSAL, the killings of Sheikh Mujib and Ziaur Rahman, and Ershad's dictatorship, up to the nineties. Her argument is that parties kept making and breaking alliances for their own benefit: the Awami League, the BNP and the Jamaat sometimes came together and sometimes faced off.

After the 2024 mass uprising, the thirty-five-year-old BNP-Jamaat alliance broke, and the two are now government and opposition. The writer says that parties switch sides easily, but ordinary supporters pay the price with their relationships.

In her view loyalty has now become a way to get favours from power. In universities, the administration, the judiciary and the media, people are known not by their work but by their political colour. Every camp stays silent on its own crimes: some on 1971, some on Operation Clean Heart, some on the deaths of 2024. Whoever asks for justice in every era becomes everyone's enemy.
The writer wants a similar survey in Bangladesh, to find out how many relationships have been sacrificed to politics since 2024, and wants intellectuals to learn to work above party identity.
nazar: This piece is from next door, but the mirror is ours too. In India as well, politics has cracked relationships, from WhatsApp groups to the dinner table, and from universities to courts loyalty is being put ahead of merit. The writer's most important point is that the demand for justice should not change depending on who is in government.
sawal: Will leaders who switch alliances answer for the broken relationships?
ref: Operation Clean Heart

An anti-crime army operation in 2002-03 under the BNP government.
Despite allegations of custodial deaths, those involved were given legal immunity.
BAKSAL

The single national party formed by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in 1975.
One-party rule in Bangladesh began with it.

h: Attacks on churches go on in Bengal, from Basanti to Malda
dek: Mobs are accused of attacking two prayer meetings in two days in South 24 Parganas and Malda, and no one has been arrested so far.
body: On the morning of 31 October, a new Church of North India church was opening in Narayantala village in the Basanti area of South 24 Parganas. Bishop Subrata Chakraborty of Barrackpore and several priests were there. According to an eyewitness, a mob of about sixty people burst in shouting slogans, smashed the phones of those filming, beat up priests and worshippers, and told women to take off their sindoor and shankha-pola (the vermilion and bangles worn by married Bengali Hindu women). It is alleged that a cross was pulled out and trampled underfoot and an elderly man was kicked.

There is an old dispute behind it too. People from a nearby Baptist church were against this building, and the bishop says it was at their urging that people from the Hindu Jagran Manch attacked. An FIR was filed, the police identified about fourteen people and sent notices to five, but no one was arrested.

The next day, a dozen people in saffron entered a Sunday prayer being held in a home in Gola Mor village in the Harishchandrapur area of Malda. According to the host, Rishi Mishra, musical instruments and speakers were smashed and people were accused of converting others with inducements. He says the police who came along did not stop the vandalism and only noted down the names of those praying.
A viral video shows a BJP leader smashing things in the house, while the VHP claims the congregation broke the items themselves. The Bajrang Dal has said five of its people were injured.
nazar: This is not an incident in one village; Alt News has been recording such attacks on Christians in Bengal for weeks. When uniforms walk with the mob and there are no arrests even after notices, freedom of worship survives only on paper. Local reports say the families in Malda who converted come from Scheduled Castes, which means the hurt is double.
sawal: If the police were there, who will answer for the broken instruments?
ref: Church of North India

A body formed in 1970 by the union of several Protestant churches.
It has several dioceses in north India, Barrackpore being one of them.

h: Megamalai: Supreme Court refuses to treat cotton farming as a forest right
dek: Of the thousands of people growing silk cotton in a tiger reserve, most now fall outside the Forest Rights Act.
body: In Tamil Nadu's Srivilliputhur-Megamalai Tiger Reserve, silk cotton (semal) has been grown on forest land for years. The state government argued that the government itself had encouraged this farming and that it could be protected under the Forest Rights Act as traditional minor forest produce. The bench of Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta did not accept this.

The court said minor forest produce is what grows on its own in the forest and what people have gathered for generations. Planned commercial farming is the opposite, and turning it into a right to live in the forest would change the very nature of the forest.

According to the government's affidavit, 4,594 people occupy more than 5,072 hectares of forest land, with cotton on 3,637 hectares. Of these, only 1,595 people live permanently inside the forest. The court refused to treat the remaining 232 who live there temporarily and the 2,767 who live outside the forest and farm inside it as claimants on the basis of farming alone.

The court has set up a committee headed by former Chief Justice B.R. Gavai to oversee the checking of claims. The remaining gram sabhas (village assemblies) will be formed in thirty days and claims must be settled in five months. The next hearing is on 1 February 2027.
nazar: The ruling speaks of saving the forest from market farming, and that point carries weight. But the real test will be whether the gram sabha process runs honestly, because the papers of genuine claimants living inside the forest often get lost in exactly these delays. About three thousand people have been pushed out at one stroke, and the question of their livelihood is nowhere to be seen in the court's order.
sawal: Why should farmers pay the price for cotton the government told them to sow?
ref: Forest Rights Act, 2006

Gives Adivasis (indigenous communities) and traditional forest dwellers living in forests rights over land and forest produce.
A non-Adivasi claimant has to show three generations, that is 75 years, of occupation before 13 December 2005.

h: A promise of ten rupees a kilo, stuck on paper
dek: Karnataka's poultry farmers have announced an indefinite strike from 25 November because an approved minimum rate has not been put into effect.
body: Two organisations of contract poultry farmers in Karnataka have announced a march to the Vidhana Soudha in Bengaluru on 25 November and an indefinite strike from that evening. During the strike, farmers will stop taking chicks from companies and raising them.

The dispute is over the 'growing charge', the amount integration companies pay a farmer for each kilo of chicken raised. In 2021 it was fixed at Rs 6.20 a kilo. Farmers were asking for at least Rs 20. After several rounds of talks with the Animal Husbandry Commissioner, an interim rate of Rs 10 a kilo was agreed, and according to one organisation the government even approved it in May 2026.

The other organisation says the order was never issued. They allege that the file got stuck during the change of Chief Minister and the new government did not direct companies to apply the rate. The companies point to the missing order and still pay the old rate.

Farmers say about 80 percent of the cost is feed, and maize and soya have become costlier, partly because maize is going into ethanol. Electricity, labour, medicines and the death of chicks in the heat are also the farmer's burden. Their demands are: the Rs 10 order, enforcement of the 2022 poultry bill, farm status for poultry rearing, and a cooperative federation like the milk federation.
nazar: In contract farming the farmer puts in the land, the shed, the electricity and the labour, but the company sets the price. When even a rate approved by the government gets lost in files, this model leaves the farmer weaker than a labourer.
sawal: Who can buy today's feed at a five-year-old rate?
ref: Integration model
The company supplies chicks, feed and medicines, and the farmer the shed and labour. The company takes away the grown birds and the farmer is paid per kilo raised.

h: Nisha Kumari Bhagat: a voice that fought for land falls silent
dek: After the death of a 38-year-old Oraon activist in Ranchi, her family and the opposition accuse the land mafia and police of harassment and are demanding a CBI inquiry.
body: Jharkhand Adivasi (indigenous) activist Nisha Kumari Bhagat, former central women's president of the Kendriya Sarna Samiti, died at her home in Ranchi on 6 November. She was 38. The police have registered a case of unnatural death.

According to the report, shortly before her death she did a Facebook live video of about 11 minutes, in which she accused the Hemant Soren government, some police officers and the land mafia of harassing her. Her family and opposition leaders are now demanding a CBI inquiry.

According to Adivasi activist Augustina Soren, Nisha had recently stood up against the alleged grabbing of about 20 acres of Adivasi land in Gumla. It is alleged that she got threatening calls from local leaders and the police to drop the matter, and that the police did not even give her a copy of her FIR. The report does not carry the government's or the police's side.

Nisha, from Raidih in Gumla, had left a corporate job in Bengaluru and come back. She fought steadily for the Sarna religion code, PESA and the CNT-SPT laws, led a 40-kilometre PESA march in 2025, and contested the 2024 election from Gumla on a JLKM ticket. Soren says such leaders are pushed forward, but left alone as soon as they clash with powerful people.
nazar: Women who defend Adivasi land fight a double battle, against the mafia outside and loneliness within. If an outspoken leader cannot even get a copy of her complaint from the police station, what hearing will an ordinary village woman get? A fair inquiry into the allegations is essential.
sawal: How much running around does it take to get one copy of an FIR?
ref: CNT-SPT laws
The Chotanagpur and Santhal Pargana Tenancy Acts, which bar the sale of Adivasi land to non-Adivasis in Jharkhand.
Sarna religion code
A long-standing demand for a separate census column for Sarna, the nature-worshipping religion of Adivasis.

h: Delivery worker attacked in Hyderabad, allegedly beaten after being asked his name
dek: Blinkit's Muslim delivery worker Habib Ansari alleges he was beaten after his religion became known, while the police call it a minor scuffle.
body: Habib Ansari, who delivers for Blinkit in Hyderabad, was attacked in Panchavati Colony around 11 pm on 3 November. Ansari, from Banka district in Bihar, has lived in the Golconda area for five years. He was returning from a delivery and had stopped on hearing screams.

Ansari alleges that as soon as six or seven people learned he was Muslim, they beat him, broke his bike, snatched his phone and a thousand rupees, and threatened to kill him if he complained. When he ran into a shop, they chased him there too and beat him. In the end local people rescued him and called the police. A video of the attack went viral.

Amjedullah Khan of the Majlis Bachao Tehreek criticised the police for three days with no FIR and no arrest. On 6 November he went to the police station with AIMIM MLA Kausar Mohiuddin Ansari. Ansari also alleges that at the Raidurgam police station itself, the accused pressured him to withdraw his complaint.

The police say an FIR has been filed, charges of assault and wrongful restraint have been brought against three named people and others, two people have been arrested and the third has not yet come forward. The police deny any communal motive and call it a fight over a small matter.
nazar: A gig worker moves alone through unknown lanes day and night, with neither a union nor any shield from the company. The police and the victim differ on the motive, but that an MLA has to go to the police station to get an FIR filed says a lot in itself.
sawal: Whose job is it to protect a worker wearing an app's uniform?
ref: Gig worker
Workers who get jobs through apps, whom companies treat as 'partners' rather than employees, so they get little of the protection of labour laws.

h: Death threats after a TV debate, High Court orders police protection
dek: Kerala journalist Aparna Kurup, who discussed a cleric's remarks on women's rights, will now get police protection.
body: On 6 November the Kerala High Court ordered the officer in charge of the Ernakulam South police station to give full protection to Aparna Kurup, senior editor at the Malayalam channel Big TV, and her minor son. The order was passed by Justice Murali Purushothaman.

The case began with a TV debate. On a programme called 'Big Dialogue', Aparna had discussed a public statement on women's rights by Islamic scholar Kanthapuram A.P. Aboobacker Musliyar. She says this was plain journalism, protected by Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. After that she faced fierce attacks on social media and got death threats.

Aparna also complained to the police, but she says the threats grew instead of stopping. She then went to court and asked for protection for herself, her son and her home, a threat assessment by the police commissioner, and a proper investigation of her complaint.

The government lawyer told the court that the station officer was ready to give protection when needed, that there was already watch near her home, and that protection was being given under the court's earlier interim order. On this basis the petition was disposed of. The court said Aparna can report any threat or attempt to intimidate her to the police station, and the police will then have to protect her and her home.
nazar: Debating a statement is a journalist's job; getting death threats for it is the sickness of our times. The court did get her protection, but the report does not say how far the investigation has reached towards those who made the threats. Until action is taken against them, a guard is only a bandage, not a cure.
sawal: The journalist got a guard; what did those who threatened her get?
ref: Article 19(1)(a)

The part of the Constitution that gives every citizen freedom of speech and expression.
Courts have also drawn freedom of the press from it.

h: Two husbands, one form: the bind of Himachal's Hattee families
dek: The jodidar custom practised in the Trans-Giri area of Sirmaur cannot be recorded in government documents, and women and children pay the price.
body: Across the Giri river in Himachal Pradesh's Sirmaur district, among the Hattee community living around the Shillai block, a woman marrying several brothers still happens. This is called the jodidar custom. This report by development researcher Syed Altamash shows that a relationship accepted by everyone inside the home disappears the moment it reaches a government form.

The report begins with 29-year-old Radhika, who was refused a room by a hotel in Jaipur because her Aadhaar records did not match her marriage. Villagers link the custom to scarce land: farms in the hills are small, and if they are split among brothers, no one is left with anything, so this became a way to keep the family and the land together.

The trouble is that Aadhaar, school records, ration cards, bank papers and marriage certificates all have room for only one husband and one father. Usually the eldest brother's name goes in and the other brothers are left out of the record. This affects the division of property, loans, adoption, children's documents, and even maintenance after divorce or separation.

Interestingly, the jodidar custom has already shown up in panchayat and revenue records, and the Himachal High Court has also recognised it. Disputes are settled in the village's traditional council, the khumli. In 2024 the High Court stayed the inclusion of the Hattee community in the Scheduled Tribes list. The Kinnaura community in Kalpa in Kinnaur faces similar problems.
The writer says the real question is not whether this custom should be seen as right or wrong, but that there is simply no arrangement to bridge the gap between a family's real life and the law.
nazar: The digital identity system is built assuming lives that fit a single mould. Families that do not fit that mould become invisible everywhere, in welfare schemes, at the bank and in court. This story is not just about the Hattees, but about all the Adivasi (indigenous) and hill communities whose customs do not fit the boxes on a form.
Reform should begin not by passing judgment on a custom, but by securing the rights of the people living in it, especially women and children.
sawal: Why does Aadhaar not recognise a relationship the village accepts?
ref: Jodidar custom
Fraternal polyandry practised among Himachal's Hattee community, in which a woman marries brothers. It is seen as a way to avoid dividing land.
Hattee community
A hill community of the Trans-Giri area of Sirmaur. In 2024 the Himachal High Court stayed the decision to give it Scheduled Tribe status.

h: Instead of burning stubble: village women are asking for work
dek: A young worker at a company that turns stubble into biogas fuel found, in villages across five states, that the first wall blocking opportunity is conversation.
body: Every November, stubble smoke mixes into north India's air and the debate gets stuck on blaming farmers. In this personal account published on Village Square, Anya Goyal shows another side: where are village women in the new ways of earning that are opening up from farm waste?

Goyal grew up in Delhi, studied entrepreneurship at Babson College in Boston, and wanted to work in farming even though she is not from a farming family. Since April she has been with a bioenergy company called FarmWatt Innovations, which asks farmers to bale their stubble instead of burning it, collects it at farm energy centres in villages and takes it to compressed biogas plants. For this work she went to more than twenty villages in each of Haryana, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh.

She had believed that rural women did not want to step out of their homes at all. The villages broke that belief. She says it was the men, not the women, who were more hesitant to talk to outsiders. At the opening of one centre, women who had not come out earlier later came on their own to ask what work they could get there, so that stubble that would have gone up in smoke could be put to use.

The writer also gives figures: according to PLFS 2023-24, about two of every three working women in the country, and more than three in four in villages, are in farming. Yet among the farmers linked to one farm digitisation project, women were only 17 percent. Farming employs about 46 percent of the country's working population, but its share of gross value added is only about 18 percent.
Her conclusion is that a lack of conversation comes before a lack of opportunity: information and openings reach men first, and women are left out of the circles where these are shared.
nazar: This is the personal experience of a writer who works for a company, not an independent investigation, so it should be read that way. Still, the point is solid: the women who carry most of the burden in the fields must be made partners, not just labourers, in new schemes like stubble management.
The answer to Delhi's smoke will not come only from fines and satellite pictures. If information and income reach village women directly, stubble can become jobs instead of waste.
sawal: Will the hands that tie the stubble bales get a share of the profit?
ref: Compressed biogas (CBG)
Gas made from organic matter like farm waste and cow dung, which is cleaned and compressed for use like CNG. The government promotes stubble as its raw material.
PLFS
The Periodic Labour Force Survey, the government's regular survey that shows how many people in the country do what kind of work and how much unemployment there is.

h: The noose and the drug trade: two neighbours, two paths
dek: Al Jazeera's 101 East film examines the punishment policies of Malaysia and Singapore through the families of two death row prisoners.
body: Malaysia and Singapore are only a bridge apart, but on the death penalty in drug cases the two countries are now moving in opposite directions. This twenty-five-minute film from Al Jazeera's weekly programme 101 East captures that gap and asks whether tough laws really stop the drug trade.

Malaysia abolished the mandatory death sentence in 2023. Before that, for some crimes, including trafficking drugs above a set quantity, a judge had no option but hanging. After the law changed, courts got the discretion to decide the sentence. According to the film, more than seven hundred drug offenders who had been sentenced to death then had their sentences reheard and were given new ones.

Malaysia is now considering going further with more reform of its drug policy. Singapore, on the other hand, is clear: its government says only tough laws keep people away from drugs. The film notes that in recent years the pace of hangings for drug trafficking in Singapore has picked up.

Going beyond figures and official arguments, the film tells the story of two people: one prisoner is in a Malaysian jail and the other in Singapore, both sentenced to death. The camera goes to their families and shows how differently two policies change the lives of families caught up in the same kind of charge: on one side a window of hope opens, on the other the wait never ends.

This debate is not new. Singapore's drug law presumes that anyone caught with more than a set quantity is a trafficker, and such cases carry the death penalty. In past years, human rights groups and UN experts strongly objected to some hangings, especially in cases where those caught were poor couriers.

The film's central question is this: if the fear of hanging worked, trafficking cases in Singapore would have fallen, and if Malaysia's leniency were wrong, things there would have got worse. Instead of forcing a direct answer, 101 East lays out the arguments on both sides and the pain of the families, and leaves the verdict to the viewer.
nazar: In India too, the NDPS Act provides for the death penalty for repeat drug offences, and after every major crime the demand for hanging becomes a political slogan. This film is a reminder that the claim that fear of the noose stops crime is not as proven as it sounds. Those caught are mostly small couriers, not the big bosses.

Malaysia's experience shows that giving discretion back to the courts is not weakness but a basic condition of justice. A society that turns punishment into a tool of revenge often places the burden on the weakest shoulders.
sawal: Mercy on one side of the bridge, the noose on the other: where is justice?
ref: Mandatory death sentence
A legal provision under which, once a crime is proven, the judge has no option but hanging. Malaysia abolished it in 2023 and gave courts discretion.
101 East
Al Jazeera English's weekly investigative programme, which makes films on society, politics and human rights issues in the Asia-Pacific region.

h: The geography of a Diwali hidden in a grandmother's odhni
dek: A simple question asked in an Udaipur kitchen takes Anjana Ratnu back to a childhood Diwali, when a little girl scared of firecrackers took shelter in her grandmother's odhni.
body: Anjana Ratnu's memoir on Hindwi's 'Bela' begins late one night before Diwali. The writer, who is doing a PhD in Udaipur, and her husband Vikram are cooking for friends who could not go home for the festival. The biryani is Vikram's job, and cooking is an excuse for the two of them to spend time together.

In the middle of this Vikram asks which was the most memorable Diwali of her life. The answer keeps getting put off, now in a hunt for a missing bottle of sharbat, now in the rush over borrowed utensils and forgotten spices. After the guests leave, watching the lights on the banks of Fateh Sagar, it seems that perhaps this night is the most memorable one.

Then a forgotten picture surfaces. A Diwali spent with her grandparents in the village at the age of seven or eight, when only two diyas (oil lamps) were burning in the house and her coughing grandmother was cooking on the chulha (clay stove). Scared by the noise of firecrackers, the little girl cried loudly and hid in her grandmother's odhni.

The writer honestly admits that some parts of this memory may have been put together later, such as the bit about her grandmother's bhindi (okra), which she had heard from her mother again and again. She also mentions an idea from psychology about how memories mix up their source. But at every frightening moment, whether an exam, a research presentation or barking dogs, it is that same odhni she remembers.

In the end a question arises: why are ancestral homes known by men's names, and why should only women carry the weight of symbols like the odhni, the ghunghat (veil) and the mangalsutra? The writer rejects these customs, yet for her the grandmother's odhni has become not a command but a safe place.
nazar: This essay is a slow, personal voice amid the noise of the festival. The writer, who studies cultural geography, measures 'place' not with a map but with the fold of a cloth, and that is its beauty.
In our view, the most precious thing is the struggle over how to hold on to the love tied to a tradition while rejecting its burden. Many women today face this question.
sawal: How do we keep the memory of a custom we reject?
ref: Odhni

A long scarf women in Rajasthan and western India use to cover the head and shoulders.
In many areas its colour and print change with community, occasion and age.
Topophilia

An idea coined by geographer Yi-Fu Tuan: a person's emotional bond with a place.
In cultural geography it is the basis for seeing place as experience, not just a map.
photo_note: Raja Ravi Varma: portrait of a woman

h: Dastan-e-BHU: a night in the hostel, a song and trust
dek: This instalment of Preeti Chaudhary's memoir draws a vivid sketch of friendship, harassment, ragging and campus mischief from memories of BHU's Old Hostel.
body: This instalment of Preeti Chaudhary's series 'Dastan-e-BHU' (The Tale of BHU) on Hindwi's 'Bela' opens with a restless night in the hostel. The writer, a first-year student, sees that her senior roommate is shattered by some humiliation and cannot sleep.

The reason comes out later. When she turned down the proposal of a boy who called himself a student leader, he sent the senior something deeply vulgar and insulting by post. The writer calls this cowardice. That night, to lift the mood, she plays a Ben E. King song from the senior's cassettes, the volume goes up, the girls next door gather, and the senior smiles again.

This leads the writer to think about companionship and trust: wanting someone by your side is not enough, trust has to be earned and kept. From Nirala and the Ashok Vatika of the Ramayana to a recent film, she shows how a voice or a picture can suddenly pull you back to a place from years ago.

The rest is full of campus bustle. Waiting for phone calls near the fountain in the days before mobiles, a famous tree where couples met, the Punjabi warden Rani Madam and a shy watchman, and a month of ragging with rules about salwar-kameez in set colours and bowing low to salute.

The writer also records that not all ragging was innocent, that some students went through deep mental distress, and that today it is a crime by law. The instalment ends at the youth festival in Swatantrata Bhawan, where whistles and catcalls drown out the stage. The story continues.
nazar: Along with the sweetness of nostalgia, this memoir does not hide the bitterness that came to girls on campus. A rejected 'leader' and an insult sent by post: this story would not seem strange on today's campuses either.
What we liked best is that the girls' sympathy for one another, through a cassette and a song, becomes the answer to humiliation.
sawal: Who is the first support for a girl facing humiliation on campus?
ref: Swatantrata Bhawan

The large auditorium of Banaras Hindu University.
Convocations, youth festivals and big events are held here.
Ben E. King

American soul and R&B singer (1938-2015).
His 1961 song 'Stand By Me' became a byword for friendship and standing by someone.

h: A book on Bijnori, Ghalib's first devotee, but the introduction is missing
dek: Rauf Parekh reads a 656-page collection on Abdur Rahman Bijnori and asks why the introduction praised over four hundred pages is not in the book itself.
body: There is a famous claim in Urdu criticism that India has two revealed books, the Vedas and the Diwan-e-Ghalib. Dr Abdur Rahman Bijnori wrote this in his introduction to Ghalib's Urdu diwan (collected poems). In his weekly Dawn column 'Literary Notes', Rauf Parekh discusses this introduction and a new book published on it.

Parekh says Bijnori's introduction is less cool criticism and more emotional praise. One critic called him 'the first Ghalib worshipper', but Parekh points out that the first book on Ghalib's life and art was Hali's 'Yadgar-e-Ghalib' (A Memoir of Ghalib), which came out in 1897.

The story is an interesting one. A handwritten copy of Ghalib's poetry from 1821 was found in a library in Bhopal in August 1918. Bijnori was preparing a new edition of the diwan at Maulvi Abdul Haq's request and had finished its introduction, but he died in November 1918. The introduction was published in 1921, first in an Urdu journal and then with the 'Nuskha-e-Hamidiya'.

Now Rang-e-Adab of Karachi has published Dr Daud Usmani's collection, which has essays on Bijnori by several critics. Parekh sees two big flaws in it. First, the essays make conflicting claims about Bijnori's date of birth, from 1885 to 1887, and the editor offers no comment on them. Second, the introduction itself, a little over a hundred pages, is not included in the book, while about four hundred pages are filled with essays repeating praise for it.
Parekh concludes that the reader closes the book still wondering what exactly that introduction says and where it can be found.
nazar: This short column catches a big malaise: in our literary world, revering elders often becomes more important than reading what they actually wrote.
In our view, bringing a hundred-year-old introduction to today's reader would have been the greatest tribute. Four hundred pages of praise cannot take its place.
sawal: Why does the real book get lost under a pile of praise?
ref: Abdur Rahman Bijnori
Urdu critic and essayist (died 1918). His introduction to Ghalib's diwan became famous as 'Mahasin-e-Kalam-e-Ghalib' (The Virtues of Ghalib's Poetry).
Nuskha-e-Hamidiya
A handwritten 1821 copy of Ghalib's early Urdu poetry, found in Bhopal in 1918 and published in 1921.
photo_note: Jahangir and Prince Khurram, a Mughal painting

h: Tagore's song and his anger over opium: a Kerala student remembers
dek: A section of Kochattil Kalyanikutty Amma's autobiography records her disillusionment with colonial schooling and hearing Rabindranath Tagore in Madras.
by: Kochattil Kalyanikutty Amma, translated by J. Devika
body: Scroll has published an extract from the autobiography of Malayalam writer and women's rights advocate Kochattil Kalyanikutty Amma. J. Devika's English translation has come out from Zubaan Books as 'Wayfarer Woman and the Wayside Lamps'.

The extract begins in her college days, when the writer began to feel that the history taught under British rule was designed to fill Indians with a sense of inferiority. It had no mention of India's knowledge, and stories like the Black Hole or Plassey were told like British boasts. When an Anglo-Indian classmate said in class that 'we' conquered India, the Indian girls openly objected.

The writer says several things broke her respect for foreign rule: Gandhi's speech in Thrissur, the Khilafat movement, the brutality with which the Mappila uprising was crushed, and accounts written about the Andaman jail. She also remembers the college's English principal as honest and fair, someone who scolded those who asked for bribes in front of everyone.

The liveliest part is about Tagore's visit to Women's Christian College in Madras. He arrived on time, wearing a yellow silk robe, left his chair to sit on the carpet, and spoke in a calm voice without moving his hands. When the students asked, after first pleading that his voice was not right, he sang the national anthem, and the writer says its sweetness was beyond words.

The next day, at a public meeting, the same calm face filled with anger when Tagore spoke about the British Opium Wars that forced opium on China. The writer accepts that Tagore disagreed with non-cooperation and the bonfires of foreign cloth, yet she calls him a matchless patriot and a close friend of Gandhi.
nazar: This extract is a reminder that nationalism was not a slogan but a long journey of learning and disillusionment, and that a girl's own eyes were part of that journey.
In our view, that double picture of Tagore, gentle while singing and stern while speaking about empire, is a lesson for today: refinement and anger can live together in the same person.
sawal: Why might it seem hard today to call Tagore, who disagreed with Gandhi, a patriot?
ref: Kochattil Kalyanikutty Amma
Kerala writer and teacher, active on women's education and rights in the early twentieth century. Her autobiography has now come out in English.
Opium Wars
Two wars Britain forced on China in the nineteenth century to keep up the trade in opium grown in India. China had to give up ports and Hong Kong.

h: When the country grows teeth: three Kannada poems of fear
dek: Three Kannada poems by Kamalakar Bhat, in his own translation, speak of today's fear through images of a biting dog, a yellow butterfly that breaks eggs and a city full of teeth.
body: Scroll's poetry corner this week has three poems by Kannada poet Kamalakar Bhat, translated into English by the poet himself. All three are poems of resistance and protest, but none shouts a slogan. All of them work through metaphor.

The first poem is about a dog that bit a child and now lunges at people in lanes, parks and homes. The poem quietly hints that this animal did not turn violent on its own. It keeps looking at the man who taught it to bite and who stands nearby holding a weapon. Violence here is not madness but something someone has trained.

The second poem has a frightening yellow butterfly that wrecks sparrows' nests and breaks their eggs, but turns meek before tall buildings and the powerful. A poor child watches it hovering over the ground in wonder, and in the end the butterfly flies off towards the sun.

The third poem is the most open. In it the country's roads, offices, stations and parks have grown teeth, and even coins have started to bite. The speaker is hiding his friendships, his songs and his joy, afraid that an order will come from above about who may touch whom, what to eat and what to feel. A burst watermelon, with no teeth inside, scares the whole lane for a moment.
nazar: Bhat's poems come at a time when police vans in cities are being filled with protesters. Their strength is that they do not name the fear but show how it is built: who teaches, who bites, and who just stands and watches.
In our view, the image of a lane scared by a burst watermelon is one of the truest pictures of this time, when even food falls under suspicion.
sawal: Why is it so important to recognise, in a poem, the one who teaches biting?
ref: Kamalakar Bhat
Kannada poet and translator, who also translates his own poems into English.
Metaphor
A way of saying something in poetry by showing one thing as another, as here the country as a city with teeth.

h: Ashok Vajpeyi remembers Rituraj: a poet who stood by others
dek: Ashok Vajpeyi's tribute to the poet Rituraj, who died at 86, sees him as a poet of humanity and companionship.
body: In his column 'Kabhi-Kabhar' (Now and Then), Ashok Vajpeyi remembers the poet Rituraj, who recently passed away at the age of 86. He begins with a poem by Rituraj more than thirty years old, in which the poet says he stopped writing, life was hard, yet he went on living and did not die.

Vajpeyi says this stopping was only a matter of the poem. In fact Rituraj kept writing steadily for decades, and writing was his very way of living. He had restlessness and calm together, no vanity at all, and a constant sense that he and everyone else were human first and last.

The writer feels that Rituraj's ideological commitment was hazy at first and grew clearer with time. This gave him an eye for experiences, characters and situations that would otherwise have been missed, but it did not reduce the sensory richness of his poetry. His poetry stands against injustice and cruelty, but does not turn away from the beauty of the world. Vajpeyi places him among the few poets of his generation who carry echoes of the Sanskrit tradition, and like Muktibodh calls him a poet of companionship.

He also lists the long line of poets of the sixties generation who have gone one by one: Dhoomil, Kamlesh, Malayaj, Rajkamal Chaudhary, Chandrakant Devtale, Vishnu Khare, Vinod Kumar Shukla, and now Rituraj. In the end the writer says Rituraj fearlessly opposed today's rulers and invited others into that fearless company too. In the rest of the column Vajpeyi writes about democracy faltering across the world and the indifference of the middle class in the face of violence.
nazar: Reading the list of a whole generation that has gone, it feels as if an era of Hindi poetry is closing before our eyes. The best invitation to read Rituraj is that in his poetry anger and beauty do not cancel each other out but walk together. In today's climate, that balance is itself a kind of resistance.
sawal: Who will join Rituraj's fearless company today?
ref: Kabhi-Kabhar

Ashok Vajpeyi's weekly column, published on The Wire Hindi.
It carries notes on literature, art and current politics.
Sahcharya (companionship)

The sense of being together and keeping company.
Vajpeyi calls it the mark of both Rituraj's and Muktibodh's poetry.
